sections.title: Authentication
sections.content:
AUTHENTICATION DESIGN
Authentication — verifying that only the account holder can use the account (vs. identity proofing, which verifies who they are at account creation).
Design must balance:
CIA Property | What It Means for Authentication
Confidentiality | Leaked credentials let a threat actor impersonate the account holder
Integrity | Mechanism must resist bypass/counterfeit credentials
Availability | Authentication must not impede workflow or be too hard to use
SOMETHING YOU KNOW (KNOWLEDGE FACTOR)
• Password — secret known only to account holder
• Passphrase — longer, multi-word password; more secure and easier to remember
• PIN — numeric or any-character code, valid for a single device only
PASSWORD POLICY CONTROLS
Policy | Purpose
Password Length | Minimum (sometimes maximum) character count
Password Complexity | Requires mixed case/numeric/non-alphanumeric, no username in password
Password Age | Forces new password after N days
Password Reuse/History | Blocks reselecting recent passwords; minimum age stops rapid cycling back to a preferred password
Aging vs. Expiration — aging: old password still works briefly but forces an immediate change; expiration: old password stops working, account disabled until reset.
NIST SP 800-63B now deprecates complexity rules, forced aging, and password hints as best practice.
Password Managers — mitigate password reuse across sites:
• User picks a manager (Windows Credential Manager, iCloud Keychain, or third-party plug-in)
• Vault secured with a master password (often cloud-synced)
• Manager generates random passwords per site's policy
• Manager validates site identity via certificate before autofilling
Risks: weak master password, vendor cloud compromise, spoofed-site autofill tricks.
MULTIFACTOR AUTHENTICATION (MFA) FACTORS
Factor | Description
Something You Have (ownership) | Smart card, key fob, smartphone generating/receiving a token
Something You Are (biometric/inherence) | Physiological (fingerprint, face) or behavioral (gait) identifiers
Somewhere You Are (location) | Geographic/IP/VLAN/port-based; used for continuous auth or access control, not primary auth
2FA = exactly two distinct factor types (e.g., password + smart card). Two knowledge factors (PIN + DOB) is not MFA.
BIOMETRIC AUTHENTICATION
Enrollment: sensor acquires sample → feature extraction module builds a template (mathematical representation) → later scans compared against it.
Metric | Meaning
FRR (False Rejection Rate / Type I / FNMR) | Legitimate user wrongly rejected
FAR (False Acceptance Rate / Type II / FMR) | Impostor wrongly accepted — usually the more serious error
CER (Crossover Error Rate) | Point where FRR = FAR; lower CER = more efficient/reliable system
Throughput | Time to enroll + time to authenticate; critical for high-traffic sites
FER (Failure to Enroll Rate) | Template could not be created for a user
Cost/Implementation | Scanner cost, mobile feasibility, privacy intrusiveness, accessibility for disabled users
Fingerprint — cheapest, most common, nonintrusive; degraded by moisture/dirt. Facial recognition — measures facial geometry; optical + infrared to defeat photo spoofing.
HARD AUTHENTICATION TOKENS
Generated within a secure cryptoprocessor; token itself is never transmitted.
Type | How It Works
Certificate-Based Authentication | Supplicant holds private key, signs a unique token; verified via public key; needs PKI
OTP (One-Time Password) | Hash of shared secret + sync seed (timestamp = TOTP, counter/HMAC = HOTP); single-use
FIDO U2F | Public/private key pair per account; no shared secret, no PKI needed
Device forms: smart cards (cert + private key + PIN, contact/NFC), OTP fobs (standalone, no computer interface), security keys (portable HSM, USB/NFC, may need PIN or fingerprint backup).
Simple static-code fobs/cards (e.g., building entry cards) are vulnerable to cloning and replay attacks.
SOFT AUTHENTICATION TOKENS
• SMS/email OTP — really "two-step verification," not true MFA (not an ownership factor); vulnerable to interception
• Authenticator app — registered via QR code/shared secret; unlocked by device credential; lower interception risk but shared-device malware risk remains
PASSWORDLESS AUTHENTICATION (FIDO2/WEBAUTHN)
• User picks a roaming authenticator (security key) or platform authenticator (Windows Hello, Face ID/Touch ID)
• Local gesture (fingerprint/face/PIN) confirms presence — validated only locally
• User registers with a relying party; authenticator generates a public/private key pair per relying party
• Challenge → private key signs confirmation → sent to relying party
• Relying party verifies with the public key
Attestation — mechanism (FIDO key, TPM) proves it's a genuine root of trust; identifies brand/model only, never a unique individual (privacy protection).

sections.title: Authorization
sections.content:
DISCRETIONARY VS. MANDATORY ACCESS CONTROL
Model | Basis | Notes
DAC (Discretionary) | Resource owner controls the ACL | Most flexible, most common (default in UNIX/Linux/Windows) — also weakest, hardest to centrally enforce, vulnerable to insider threats
MAC (Mandatory) | Security clearance labels/classifications | Nondiscretionary — rules can't be changed by any subject; often adds compartments (e.g., Secret + HR); enforces "write up, read down" (can't republish at a lower clearance)
ROLE- AND ATTRIBUTE-BASED ACCESS CONTROL
Model | Basis
RBAC (Role-Based) | Permissions tied to job-function roles; principals gain rights implicitly via role assignment, not explicit grants
Security Groups | Discretionary approximation of RBAC — admin-assigned group membership, not system-determined
ABAC (Attribute-Based) | Most fine-grained — combines subject/object/context attributes (OS, IP, patch status, time, location); supports M-of-N control, separation of duties
Rule-Based Access Control | Any model enforced by system rules rather than users (RBAC, ABAC, MAC all qualify); e.g., conditional access (UAC, sudo)
LEAST PRIVILEGE
Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) — minimum sufficient rights for the task. Design phase analyzes workflows to set roles/permissions.
• Too restrictive → support burden, lost productivity
• Too permissive → malware/breach risk
• Authorization creep — rights accumulate over time (direct grants or group additions) without being revoked; controlled via ongoing auditing
USER ACCOUNT PROVISIONING
Step | Purpose
Identity Proofing | Verify identity via documents/records; may include background check
Issuing Credentials | User selects password / enrolls biometric or token
Issuing Hardware/Software | Prevents shadow IT from inadequate resourcing
Teaching Policy Awareness | Security training, personal-use policy
Creating Permissions Assignment | Map work role to RBAC/MAC/ABAC rights; flag privileged accounts for monitoring
Deprovisioning — remove roles/groups on termination/project end; disable then delete, or delete immediately.
Account = unique SID + name + credential + profile (attributes, home folder, app settings). Windows access policies configured via GPOs, linked to sites/domains/OUs.
ACCOUNT RESTRICTIONS
Location-Based:
• IP address / subnet / VLAN / OU restricts logical location
• Geolocation: IP-to-map lookup (via ISP registrant data, e.g. GeoIP) or location services (GPS/cell/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth triangulation)
Time-Based:
Policy | Effect
Time-of-day restrictions | Authorized login hours only
Duration-based login | Max session length
Impossible travel time / risky login | Flags logins geographically infeasible within the elapsed time
Temporary permissions | Auto-removes role/group membership after a set period
PRIVILEGED ACCESS MANAGEMENT (PAM)
Privileged account — can reconfigure hosts, disable security controls, manage infrastructure/apps/databases.
• Restrict number of admin accounts (fewer = smaller attack surface); never share/use default accounts (kills accountability)
• SAW (Secure Administrative Workstation) — minimal-app, low-attack-surface machine for privileged sign-in
Just-in-Time (JIT) / Zero Standing Privileges (ZSP) models — elevated rights not standing, granted only on request:
Model | Mechanism
Temporary Elevation | UAC / sudo — time-limited elevation
Password Vaulting/Brokering | Credential "checked out" from a repository with logged justification; supports M-of-N approval
Ephemeral Credentials | Account generated/enabled for the task, then destroyed/disabled
Applies to human admins and service accounts.

sections.title: Identity Management
sections.content:
LOCAL AUTHENTICATION
Passwords stored as cryptographic hashes, never plaintext, to limit compromise risk.
OS | Mechanism
Windows local sign-in | LSASS compares hash to SAM database (registry) — "interactive logon"
Windows network sign-in | LSASS → AD domain controller, via Kerberos (preferred) or legacy NTLM
Windows remote sign-in | Via VPN, enterprise Wi-Fi, or web portal
Linux local | Account names in /etc/passwd, password hash in /etc/shadow
Linux network | SSH, optionally using cryptographic keys instead of password
PAM (Pluggable Authentication Module) | Linux framework enabling alternate providers (smart card, network directory)
DIRECTORY SERVICES
Directory service — stores users/computers/groups/services as objects with attributes defined by a schema; most based on LDAP (from X.500 standard).
Distinguished Name (DN) — unique identifier built from attribute-value pairs, most-specific first (the relative distinguished name).
Attribute | Meaning
CN | Common Name
OU | Organizational Unit
O | Organization
C | Country
DC | Domain Component
Example: CN=WIDGETWEB, OU=Marketing, O=Widget, C=UK, DC=widget, DC=foo
KERBEROS SSO
Single Sign-On (SSO) — authenticate once, get authorization across compatible servers without re-entering credentials.
Kerberos — SSO protocol built on a Key Distribution Center (KDC) with two services: Authentication Service (AS) and Ticket Granting Service (TGS). Users/services are collectively principals.
Authentication phase:
• Principal requests a TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) from the AS, encrypting timestamp with password hash
• AS validates and responds with the TGT (encrypted with KDC's secret key) + a TGS session key (encrypted with user's password hash)
Authorization phase:
• Principal sends TGS its TGT + target server name + an authenticator (time-stamped, encrypted with TGS session key)
• TGS responds with a Service session key + a Service ticket (info about principal, encrypted with the app server's secret key)
• Principal forwards the service ticket + a new authenticator to the application server
• Server decrypts, validates, may echo back the timestamp (encrypted w/ service session key) for mutual authentication (defeats on-path attacks)
• Server responds to requests per its ACL
Drawback: KDC is a single point of failure — mitigated with multiple domain controllers.
FEDERATION
Federation — trusting accounts managed by a different (partner/external) network, avoiding the need to manage those accounts locally.
Claims-based identity flow:
• Principal accesses a Service Provider (SP) → redirected to an Identity Provider (IdP)
• Principal authenticates with IdP, receives a signed claim (token)
• Principal presents claim to SP; SP trusts IdP's signature
• SP maps the authenticated principal to its own permissions/attributes
Protocol | Key Facts
SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) | XML-based claims; transported via HTTP/HTTPS + SOAP; signed with XML signature spec; example: AWS as SAML service provider
OAuth (Open Authorization) | For RESTful APIs; user (resource owner) grants an OAuth client limited access without sharing password; resource server hosts user data, authorization server issues tokens; client registers with an ID (public) + secret (confidential) + redirect URL; uses JWT (JSON Web Token, Base64-encoded, digitally signable) for claims

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
• Assess CIA requirements for the authentication context (private network, public web, VPN gateway, physical site).
• Determine whether MFA or passwordless authentication is required, and select ownership (smart card, OTP fob/key, authenticator app), biometric (evaluated by FAR/FRR/CER/speed/accessibility), or two-step verification (SMS/call/email/push) methods; consider password managers for stronger password-based auth.
• Choose an access control model — discretionary, mandatory, role-based, or attribute-based — accounting for whether scope includes federated on-premises/cloud services.
• Configure accounts/roles/resources using the principle of least privilege.
• Configure account policies: credential policies (secure password selection, standard vs. privileged accounts) and conditional access based on location/time.
• Establish secure provisioning procedures for issuing digital identities and credentials.
• Establish deprovisioning procedures to remove access when employees/contractors leave.
• Implement SAML or OAuth to enable SSO between on-premises networks and cloud services/applications.

concept_cards.hook: An authentication mechanism that allows a user to present a smart card to operate an entry system.
Policy that prevents access to an account under certain conditions, such as excessive failed authentication attempts.
Tracking authorized usage of a resource or use of rights by a subject and alerting when unauthorized use is detected or attempted.
Access control technique evaluating a set of attributes each subject possesses.

practice_questions.q: Creating accounts for a new employee with the access their role needs is called:
practice_questions.explanation: Provisioning sets up identities and access.

practice_questions.q: When an employee leaves, their accounts are disabled the same day. What is this?
One login lets a user reach email, HR and file storage without signing in again. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: SSO uses one authentication for many services.

practice_questions.q: A company lets a partner's employees log in to its portal using the partner's own identity system. What is this?
practice_questions.explanation: Federation trusts identities from another organization.

practice_questions.q: Which XML-based standard is commonly used for web SSO between an identity provider and a service provider?
An app asks permission to read a user's calendar from another service without getting the user's password. Which standard is this?
practice_questions.explanation: OAuth grants delegated authorization with tokens.

practice_questions.q: Access is granted based on job role, such as 'Nurse' or 'Accountant'. What model is this?
The owner of a file decides who else can access it. Which access model is this?
Access is determined by security labels such as Secret and Top Secret, which users cannot change. Which model is this?
practice_questions.explanation: MAC uses labels enforced by the system.

practice_questions.q: Access depends on several characteristics such as department, location and device type. Which model is this?
